0.1: The cost of intelligence falls ten times a year. Demand rises faster. So executives keep asking the same questions about where the money goes.
0.2: Those answers shouldn’t live in a spreadsheet someone builds later. In Akka they sit right next to the system. Here are seven questions, in the order a finance leader asks them.
1.1: The Overview starts with four figures: cost to date, the projected cost at period end against the owner’s budget, realized savings, and potential savings. Click one, and you are in the analysis behind it.
1.2: Costs breaks the same money down by use case, model, team, app, or any tag. The whole setup lives in the address, so a finance lead can bookmark it. And usage without a price is footnoted, never hidden.
1.3: Compare two periods and it reads like a financial statement. Cost rose by one hundred four dollars and seventy cents, and the bridge shows why: volume, model mix, prompt size, cache use, response size and price. The pieces add up to the cent. And one use case, ticket triage, nearly tripled after a model change.
2.1: Savings finds avoidable cost: prompts that skip the cache, failed attempts, duplicate requests, reasoning above the median, unused tool definitions, and answers that run long. Each opportunity shows a saving range, its quality risk, and the evidence behind it.
2.2: Pick a model and the console prices the period’s real traffic on it. A new price list works the same way: you see the effect, model by model, before anything is published.
2.3: For each use case, the frontier plots cost against pass rate. The owner sets the quality bar: a reference model, a judge, a tolerance, and hard gates that come from Verify. A cheaper model is only proposed when it clears the bar. Here the smaller model costs under a fifth as much and passes at ninety point two percent against ninety-one point six.
3.1: A change is tried on recorded traffic first, then staged. The owner sets the stop rule in advance, so a failing rollout halts on its own, and nobody gets paged. Continue and Keep each record who decided, and why.
3.2: The ledger keeps the estimate next to what was actually measured. Four changes landed within their estimates. One fell short, and the ledger says so.
4.1: Every budget has an owner, a plan to date, and a forecast with its range, and it names the day the money runs out. The owner sets the thresholds in advance: notify, reroute, or block.
4.2: If you host a model yourself, the worksheet gives you an assigned price, utilization, and break-even. And Prices shows what is in force and what is not costed, so every figure traces back to a price.
5.1: Cost is one part of one loop. A change is specified, built, verified, and run on the right model, with one evidence record behind it.
5.2: Seven questions, answered where the work happens.
